what: The nightly cap over candidate lists a real night did not produce: both release directions, both sides overflowing, and each side empty.
whatItCannotSay: Nothing about how many candidates a night actually has. That is what the calibration run at 2.11 measures. These say the release rule is arithmetic rather than a preference, which is the half no fixture can show while the fixture records no passing setup at all.
whyAuthored: The captured day records two setups and neither clears every gating check, so the cap over the fixture caps nothing. A rule that only ever ran on an empty list is a rule nothing has tested.

scenarios.name: both-under
scenarios.why: neither side fills its own allocation, so nothing is released and nothing is truncated

scenarios.name: exact
scenarios.why: both sides exactly full, the one arrangement where release and truncation are both zero at the boundary

scenarios.name: long-overflows
scenarios.why: the short side leaves fifteen and the long side takes them, which is the release running one way

scenarios.name: short-overflows
scenarios.why: the long side leaves thirty and the short side takes them, which is the release running the other way

scenarios.name: both-overflow
scenarios.why: neither side releases anything, so each is held to its own allocation and the split holds

scenarios.name: long-empty
scenarios.why: a night with no long candidates at all gives the whole sixty to the short side

scenarios.name: short-empty
scenarios.why: and the mirror, which is the common one in a strong market

scenarios.name: one-short-of-each
scenarios.why: one under each allocation, so two slots go unused rather than being released to a side that does not want them

ordering.why: Ranked on give-up distance in daily-range units, ascending, with ticker alphabetical breaking a tie so the boundary does not depend on the order rows came back in. Ranked within a direction and never across.
